1538.title: TLS Handshake
1538.heading: TLS Handshake
1538.content:
A TLS handshake establishes a protected session before ordinary application data is exchanged. The client and server identify supported cryptographic choices, the server presents identity evidence, and the endpoints derive session keys for encrypted communication.

Identity verification and key negotiation are separate responsibilities within the exchange. A connection is not trustworthy merely because encryption was selected; the client must also validate that the certificate identifies the intended server.

1541.content:
A tissue-on-a-chip recreates a focused tissue unit or process at microscale, such as connective-tissue wound closure or muscle contraction. The platform controls geometry and stimuli while allowing repeated imaging and measurement.

Compared with an organ model, its narrower target can simplify interpretation, though it omits interactions that emerge only across several tissues.

1544.title: Tissue Vascularization
1544.heading: Tissue Vascularization
1544.content:
Tissue vascularization creates blood-vessel-like networks that deliver oxygen and nutrients and remove waste throughout a thick construct. Passive diffusion reaches only a short distance, leaving central cells in a large solid tissue without adequate support.

Printed perfusable channels are an intermediate solution, while successful implantation ultimately requires connection with the host's circulation.

1547.title: Tissue Scaffold
1547.heading: Tissue Scaffold
1547.content:
A tissue scaffold is a temporary or persistent structure that gives cells a three-dimensional surface or volume in which to attach, organize, and deposit their own matrix. Its pores and mechanics influence transport and cell behavior.

An effective scaffold supports early function and degrades or integrates at a rate compatible with formation of new tissue.

1550.title: Tissue Engineering
1550.heading: Tissue Engineering
1550.content:
Tissue engineering combines living cells, supporting materials, fabrication, and conditioning to restore or replace damaged biological tissue. The engineered construct must reproduce enough structure and function to survive, integrate, and improve the target condition.

Different tissues impose different requirements for geometry, stiffness, electrical behavior, mechanical loading, vascularization, and cell source.

1553.title: Tissue Bioreactor
1553.heading: Tissue Bioreactor
1553.content:
A tissue bioreactor maintains engineered tissue while controlling media flow, temperature, gases, biochemical composition, and sometimes mechanical or electrical stimulation. It can improve nutrient transport and reproduce aspects of the body's operating environment.

The chamber and flow path must support sterile handling while exposing the tissue to consistent, measurable conditions.

1556.title: Timebox
1556.heading: Timebox
1556.content:
A timebox is a fixed maximum duration for an activity. When the limit is reached, participants use the best available result, stop, or explicitly replan instead of allowing the activity to expand indefinitely.

Timeboxing creates focus and a dependable inspection rhythm. Sprints, planning, Daily Scrums, reviews, and retrospectives use different timeboxes appropriate to their purpose.

Time-to-market agility is the ability to make a product or service available sooner by reducing the delay required to obtain and prepare computing environments. On-demand infrastructure and platforms can replace part of the procurement and installation sequence.

The benefit can be expressed as elapsed time or as revenue available during the months gained. Speed has value only if the service still meets its functional, security, continuity, and quality requirements.

1562.title: Time-Unrolled Recurrent Network
1562.heading: Time-Unrolled Recurrent Network
1562.content:
Unrolling a [[Recurrent Neural Network]] through time draws its repeated computation as a sequence of hidden and output layers, one set for each input step. The hidden state produced at one step becomes part of the input to the next. This drawing exposes the dependency chain that the compact recurrent loop conceals.

The apparent many-layer network does not learn independent parameters for every drawn step: the recurrent connections reuse the same weights. Unrolling makes [[Backpropagation Through Time]] easier to understand because an error at a later output must travel backward through the earlier states that influenced it.

1568.title: Time-Sharing
1568.heading: Time-Sharing
1568.content:
Time-sharing lets many terminal users interact with one large computer by rapidly dividing processor attention among them. Because machine operations are much faster than human reactions, each person can receive responses that feel immediate.

The model made scarce computing resources accessible and encouraged conversational software. Scaling it required sophisticated scheduling, memory protection, and operating systems.

A time-to-event variable measures elapsed time from a defined origin to an event or the end of observation. For participants with the event, it records the event time; for censored participants, it records their last known event-free time.

The origin, units, and maximum study window must be consistent across records. If event timing is missing for most event-positive participants, exclusions can create severe [[Survival Data Selection Bias]].

A time-series pattern dictionary represents a series by counts or weights of recurring local patterns. Windows are often normalized, discretized, and converted into symbolic words before their occurrences are accumulated.

The dictionary discards exact timing while preserving which shapes recur, producing a bag-of-patterns representation. Window length, discretization, and vocabulary construction control the balance between invariance and detail.

1583.content: A time-series scatterplot matrix displays every pairwise relationship among variables in a multivariate [[Time Series]]. Repeated panels let viewers compare correlation, curvature, clusters, and unusual observations across variable pairs. Time is not inherently visible in the positions, so [[Temporal Color Encoding]] can distinguish periods or groups. The matrix scales poorly with the number of variables because each added variable creates a new row and column of panels.

It can combine background regions, reference lines, raw curves, points, and text in a deliberate order. Because the high-level plot has already performed subsetting and scale calculations, the panel function receives the panel's coordinates and grouping information. It therefore provides a reusable mechanism for [[Layered Time-Plot Annotation]] across multiple series.

A time-series interval feature summarizes a selected contiguous segment with measures such as its mean, standard deviation, or slope. Different intervals expose localized changes without requiring an exact pattern match.

Candidate intervals may be sampled or searched at multiple lengths and positions. Many overlapping intervals create redundancy, so selection or ensemble methods are commonly used to retain useful regional information.

1595.content:
A time-harmonic electromagnetic field oscillates sinusoidally at a single angular frequency. Phasor notation separates the common exponential time factor from the spatially varying complex field amplitude.

Time differentiation then becomes multiplication by the imaginary frequency factor, converting time-domain Maxwell equations into frequency-domain equations. This form is widely used for steady sinusoidal electrical systems.

1598.heading: Time-Series Feature Representation
1598.content:
Time-series feature representation turns an ordered sequence of observations into variables suitable for comparison, prediction, or classification. It may summarize an entire series, describe selected intervals, or record the presence of local patterns.

No single representation preserves every useful aspect of temporal data. Global summaries capture overall behavior, while shapelets and pattern dictionaries retain localized structure that aggregate statistics can miss.

Time-series characterization describes a series through interpretable properties such as distribution, dependence, predictability, stationarity, and model fit. The resulting feature vector permits conventional learning algorithms to operate on whole time series.

Characterization is especially useful for heterogeneous collections because series of unequal length can be compared in a common feature space. Its success depends on selecting measures that reflect the temporal behaviors relevant to the task.

A time-dependent forcing function specifies how an applied structural load changes with time. It drives a transient response whose displacement history depends on load shape, duration, stiffness, mass, damping, and boundary conditions.

Finite element software samples or integrates the forcing history over analysis time steps. The step interval must be small enough to represent abrupt changes and the structural frequencies of interest.

1613.heading: Time Series Missing-Value Handling
1613.content: Missing-value handling for a [[Time Series]] must respect temporal order. `na.omit` removes incomplete observations, `na.contiguous` keeps the longest uninterrupted run, `na.approx` interpolates between neighboring values, and `na.locf` carries the last observation forward. The choice affects both the apparent pattern and later displays, so an imputed value should not be treated as an actual measurement.

1616.title: Time Series Shapelet Classification
1616.heading: Time Series Shapelet Classification
1616.content:
Time series shapelet classification uses short subsequences whose presence or close match is highly discriminative of a class. A candidate shapelet is compared with every possible window in a series, and the minimum distance becomes a feature or split criterion.

Shapelets provide localized explanations because the prediction can identify the characteristic segment. Searching the enormous space of possible subsequences requires pruning, sampling, or other acceleration.

The minimum distance from a candidate shapelet to all same-length windows in a series can become a derived feature. A shapelet transform therefore converts variable temporal structure into a conventional tabular representation while preserving a discriminative local form.

1631.title: Time Ramping with Optical Flow
1631.heading: Time Ramping with Optical Flow
1631.content: Time remapping compresses or stretches sections of a clip between keyframes to make action speed up or slow down. Slow motion needs new intermediate frames; simple frame blending can ghost moving subjects. Optical flow estimates pixel motion to synthesize the in-between images, but crossing or overlapping limbs can confuse it and create smears. The book suggests isolating troublesome components with mattes, ramping them separately, and recombining them when a severe speed change breaks the automatic interpolation. Temporal repair is another form of constrained scene finishing.

1634.title: Time Plot
1634.heading: Time Plot
1634.content: A time plot places a [[Time Index]] on the horizontal axis and observation values on the vertical axis, usually joining successive observations with a line. It makes direction, cycles, abrupt changes, and gaps visible in their temporal order. Multiple variables may require separate panels with [[Independent Panel Scales]], while annotations such as an [[Average-Comparison Time Plot]] can give the line a meaningful reference.

1637.title: Time Dilation
1637.heading: Time Dilation
1637.content: In special relativity, a clock moving relative to an inertial observer is measured to run slowly. If $\Delta\tau$ is the proper time recorded with the events at one location, then $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$, where $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$. The effect is reciprocal between inertial frames and becomes large near light speed.

1640.title: Time Index
1640.heading: Time Index
1640.content: A time index is the ordered set of temporal coordinates attached to the observations of a [[Time Series]]. The `zoo` model only requires the index to be totally ordered, so it can use dates, date-times, years, or specialized classes such as [[yearmon Time Index]]. Separating the index from [[zoo Core Data]] allows the same measurements to be selected, merged, plotted, or aggregated according to time.

1643.title: Time Complexity
1643.heading: Time Complexity
1643.content:
Time complexity describes how the number of elementary operations performed by an [[Algorithm]] grows with [[Input Size]]. Counting operations avoids tying the analysis to the clock speed of one computer.

Actual runtime still depends on hardware and implementation, but growth rate predicts how the same implementation will behave at larger scales. [[Big O Notation]] expresses an asymptotic upper bound and groups algorithms into useful families for comparison.

1646.title: Throughput
1646.heading: Throughput
1646.content:
Throughput is the number of work items completed per unit of time. It measures the output of a workflow rather than how busy each person or stage appears.

Together with [[Cycle Time]] and work-in-progress levels, throughput helps a team evaluate whether changes improve the whole flow. Item sizes must remain comparable enough for the count to be meaningful.

1649.title: Tiered Pricing
1649.heading: Tiered Pricing
1649.content:
Tiered pricing assigns different prices to defined bands of spending, volume, or service quality. A larger number of users may receive a lower price per user, while a stricter service-level tier may carry a higher charge.

The boundaries and measurement period determine which tier applies. This approach can reward scale or let consumers choose among service commitments without requiring the provider to create a completely different offering for every customer.

1652.title: Timation Program
1652.heading: Timation Program
1652.content: Timation was a Naval Research Laboratory program for transferring precise time and testing satellite ranging. Its first two satellites used quartz oscillators and side-tone ranging, while the third mission evolved into Navigation Technology Satellite 1 and carried atomic clocks. Timation demonstrated the core architectural idea that synchronized clocks could reside in medium-Earth-orbit satellites and broadcast timing from which users determined range.

1655.title: Tile Map
1655.heading: Tile Map
1655.content:
A tile map represents a two-dimensional level as a grid of references to reusable images in a tile set. The map stores which tile belongs at each location, while the tile set stores the actual visual assets.

This separation makes large levels compact and editable. Additional layers can represent background, terrain, objects, and foreground elements, with the [[2D Painter's Algorithm]] determining their drawing order.

1657.sourceSearchName: threshold logic unit threshold logic unit
1657.title: Threshold Logic Unit
1657.heading: Document

1658.sourceSearchName: threshold logic unit threshold logic unit
1658.title: Threshold Logic Unit
1658.heading: Threshold Logic Unit
1658.content:
A threshold logic unit sums weighted inputs and emits a high or low output depending on whether that sum crosses a fixed threshold. Kelleher describes early neural models that used Boolean inputs and outputs to represent logical relations. The McCulloch–Pitts model could implement simple operations such as conjunction and disjunction with hand-set excitatory or inhibitory weights.

Adding a learning rule led toward the [[Perceptron]], but a single threshold unit still creates a linear decision boundary. Its abrupt [[Activation Function|threshold activation]] also lacks the derivative required by ordinary [[Backpropagation]]. These limits help explain why later multilayer training used smoother activations.

1659.sourceSearchName: threshold logic unit threshold logic unit

1661.content:
Three-point lighting arranges key, fill, and back lights around a subject. The key establishes the main direction, the fill moderates its shadows, and the back light separates the subject from the background.

The arrangement is a starting point rather than a rigid formula. Changing relative angle and intensity can move the scene from even studio illumination toward stark shadows, silhouettes, or other dramatic effects.

1664.title: Threshold Highlighting
1664.heading: Threshold Highlighting
1664.content: Threshold highlighting marks the time intervals in which a series satisfies a condition, such as temperature falling below a reference or radiation exceeding a limit. A shaded background block lets viewers compare the duration and timing of qualifying intervals while the original [[Time Plot]] remains visible. The threshold defines an analytical statement, so its value and direction should be explained rather than left as an unexplained color change.

1667.heading: Three-Dimensional Scene Reconstruction
1667.content:
Three-dimensional scene reconstruction builds a geometrically plausible arrangement of cameras, objects, support surfaces, and bodies that could project to the observed photograph. Known sizes, contact points, articulation limits, and perspective cues turn otherwise ambiguous image measurements into testable spatial relationships.

The method can reveal that a person would need an implausible size or pose to occupy the claimed location. Its conclusion depends on the assumed dimensions and camera model, so sensitivity analysis is needed to show that the inconsistency persists across reasonable alternatives.

1670.heading: Three-Node Bar Element
1670.content:
A three-node bar element adds a midside node between two end nodes and uses quadratic displacement interpolation. Each node still carries one axial translational degree of freedom.

The higher-order field can represent distributed loading and linearly varying cross section more accurately than one linear element. A coarser mesh of quadratic elements may therefore match the accuracy of many two-node elements.

Thicker constructs are harder to image and feed, and passive diffusion creates a limit on how far oxygen and nutrients reach living cells.

1688.title: Threat Assessment
1688.heading: Threat Assessment
1688.content:
A threat assessment identifies the kinds of harmful events, actors, or conditions to which an organization and its information may be exposed. It considers attacks from outside, misuse from inside, compromised clients, interrupted providers, and failures along the data journey.

The result informs [[Security Risk]] and the selection of preventive, detective, and recovery controls. Threats should be reassessed when a cloud deployment changes its users, locations, service providers, interfaces, or stored data.

A cybersecurity assessment begins by identifying valuable information assets, then enumerates [[Cyber Threat|threats]] and [[Cyber Vulnerability|vulnerabilities]] that could affect them. Likelihood and impact ratings provide a defensible basis for prioritizing scarce defensive resources.

1694.title: Thomson Effect
1694.heading: Thomson Effect
1694.content: The Thomson effect is heat released or absorbed along a single current-carrying material that also has a temperature gradient. Its direction changes when current reverses, so the source treats it as reversible. This distributed heat exchange differs from the junction-localized [[Peltier Effect]] and from irreversible [[Joule Heating]]. It matters when accounting for thermal flow through thermoelectric legs.

1706.title: Thin Client
1706.heading: Thin Client
1706.content:
A thin client is a user device that retains a local operating system but depends on remotely hosted applications, data, or computation for much of its useful work. It provides an interface to services instead of running and maintaining every application locally.

Centralizing applications can reduce endpoint hardware and support requirements and limit data stored on a lost device. The client becomes more dependent on network access and the availability of the remote service.

1709.heading: Thin Lens Equation
1709.content:
The thin lens equation relates object distance $u$, image distance $v$, and focal length $f$ through a consistent sign convention:

$$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}.$$

Ray diagrams determine whether the image is real or virtual and its orientation, while magnification follows from the ratio of image to object dimensions.

1712.title: Thermopile
1712.heading: Thermopile
1712.content: A thermopile connects multiple thermocouple or thermoelectric pairs in series so their Seebeck voltages add. It raises output voltage without requiring a single pair to span a larger temperature difference. The source presents this arrangement as one way to make a [[Thermoelectric Generator]] more useful for a load. Each pair still has its own material and heat-leak constraints.

1715.heading: Thermogravimetric Thermal Analysis
1715.content:
Thermogravimetric analysis records a sample's mass as temperature changes through a prescribed heating cycle. A decline in mass can identify degradation or evaporation and thereby establish an upper processing-temperature limit.

Coupling the measurement with evolved-gas analysis can also identify the composition and timing of released vapor. These observations define material transitions that a [[Temperature-Dependent Thermophysical Properties|temperature-dependent model]] should not silently extrapolate through.

1718.title: Thermoelectric Material Selection
1718.heading: Thermoelectric Material Selection
1718.content: Selecting generator legs means seeking a large [[Seebeck Coefficient]], good electrical conduction, and low thermal leakage at the intended hot-side temperature. The source favors suitable p-type and n-type semiconductors over ordinary metals and also requires strength, corrosion resistance, and compatible conducting bridges. Doping and geometry can improve the [[Thermoelectric Figure of Merit]], but thermal stress can still limit service life.

1721.heading: Thermodynamic Weather Diagrams
1721.content: Stüve diagrams, emagrams, tephigrams, and skew-T log-P diagrams plot atmospheric temperature and pressure in forms chosen to make parcel processes easier to interpret. A vertical sounding can show environmental temperature, dew point, adiabatic paths, and moisture relationships on one chart. These diagrams support identification of [[Lifted Condensation and Convection Levels]] and layers of stability or instability.

1724.title: Thermoelectric Generator
1724.heading: Thermoelectric Generator
1724.content: A thermoelectric generator places p-type and n-type elements between a hot and a cold junction. The [[Seebeck Effect]] makes an electrical potential from that temperature difference and a connected load receives power. Heat also leaks by conduction, and current incurs [[Joule Heating]] and other thermoelectric heat exchanges. Material properties and load resistance jointly determine efficiency and output.

1727.sourceSearchName: thermoelectric figure of merit thermoelectric figure of merit
1727.title: Thermoelectric Figure of Merit
1727.heading: Thermoelectric Figure of Merit
1727.content: Figure of merit $Z$ combines the useful [[Seebeck Coefficient]] with unwanted electrical resistance and thermal conduction of a thermoelectric pair. The source expresses it as a squared differential coefficient divided by the product of total electrical and thermal paths; higher $Z$ improves attainable efficiency. The dimensionless $ZT$ includes operating temperature. No single material property can be optimized in isolation.

1736.title: Thermionic Reactor Integration
1736.heading: Thermionic Reactor Integration
1736.content: Nuclear-reactor fuel elements can provide the high-temperature side of a [[Thermionic Generator]]. A hot fuel-associated emitter is surrounded by a cooler collector, with an ionized gap to carry electrons and reduce space charge. Electrical power is extracted directly from some heat near the reactor source. Cooling, radiation environment, electrode durability, and material protection still determine whether the arrangement is practical.

1737.sourceSearchName: thermionic reactor integration thermionic reactor integration
1737.title: Thermionic Reactor Integration
1737.heading: References

1739.title: Thermionic Generator
1739.heading: Thermionic Generator
1739.content: A thermionic generator heats an emitter until it releases electrons, guides them across a narrow vacuum or ionized-vapor gap, and collects them on a cooler electrode. The electrons return through an external load, producing electrical power. It has no moving conversion parts, but high emitter temperature, [[Space-Charge Barrier]], heat rejection, and electrode materials govern its practical efficiency.

1742.title: Thermionic Emitter
1742.heading: Thermionic Emitter
1742.content: The emitter is the hot cathode of a [[Thermionic Generator]]. Its surface must reach a temperature at which electrons can overcome the [[Surface Work Function]] and leave for the collector. Low work function helps emission, but the electrode also needs to survive the heat and corrosive surroundings. The source identifies expensive high-temperature materials and protective ceramic shielding as design limitations.

1745.title: Thermionic Emission
1745.heading: Thermionic Emission
1745.content: Thermionic emission releases electrons from a heated solid surface once some electrons gain enough energy to cross its [[Surface Work Function]] barrier. The emitted electrons can move through a vacuum or conductive vapor gap to a cooler collector. This makes emission a direct heat-to-electron-current mechanism, although a working [[Thermionic Generator]] also needs an external return path and manageable space charge.

1747.sourceSearchName: thermionic conversion efficiency thermionic conversion efficiency
1747.title: Thermionic Conversion Efficiency
1747.heading: Document

1748.sourceSearchName: thermionic conversion efficiency thermionic conversion efficiency
1748.title: Thermionic Conversion Efficiency
1748.heading: Thermionic Conversion Efficiency
1748.content: Thermionic conversion efficiency is electrical load power divided by heat supplied to the emitter. It remains below the ideal heat-engine limit set by hot-emitter and cool-collector temperatures because emission, collector rejection, gap transport, radiation, and other losses consume part of the input. The source's worked example contrasts a much lower actual device efficiency with its Carnot limit. High current density alone therefore does not establish high efficiency.

1749.sourceSearchName: thermionic conversion efficiency thermionic conversion efficiency
1749.title: Thermionic Conversion Efficiency
1749.heading: References

1751.title: Thermionic Collector
1751.heading: Thermionic Collector
1751.content: The collector is the cooler anode that receives electrons crossing from the [[Thermionic Emitter]]. Electrons give up energy at its surface, so collector heat must be rejected while they return through the external load. Its temperature and surface work function affect the useful voltage. The source discusses cesium-coated collector materials as one approach, alongside the need to control the gap's [[Space-Charge Barrier]].

1754.sourceSearchName: thermionic boiler tube integration thermionic boiler tube integration
1754.title: Thermionic Boiler-Tube Integration
1754.heading: Thermionic Boiler-Tube Integration
1754.content: A boiler riser tube receives strong radiation from combustion gases and can be fitted with thermionic emitter and collector surfaces. This extracts some electricity from high-temperature heat before the remaining energy drives a steam plant. The source fills the electrode gap with ionized cesium vapor. The integration is a topping approach, not a replacement for the boiler's fluid and downstream turbine cycle.

A closed thermal system permits energy as heat or work to cross its boundary while retaining its mass. Its boundary may move or deform, but the same collection of matter remains the object of the balance.

A control volume occupies a defined region through which both mass and energy may flow. Selecting between these viewpoints determines whether advected enthalpy must appear alongside conduction, generation, work, and storage in the [[Energy Conservation in Thermal Continua|energy balance]].

A numerical solver substitutes an approximate field into the assembled equations and measures the remaining imbalance as a residual. Iteration continues until the residual meets a defined tolerance or another stopping condition is reached.

Convergence only shows that the discretized equations were solved to the chosen criterion; it does not prove that the equations, mesh, properties, or conditions represent reality. Residual plots therefore complement, rather than replace, [[Verification versus Validation in Thermal Modeling|verification and validation]].

1766.heading: Thermal Property Unit Conversion
1766.content: Thermal-property units combine energy or power with area, length, mass, and temperature intervals in different positions. The book writes thermal conductivity in W/(m·K), heat-transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K), heat capacity in kJ/K, and specific heat capacity in kJ/(kg·K). These are not one interchangeable heat unit: the extra length, area, or mass changes the dimension. In compound conversions, Fahrenheit-to-kelvin interval ratios are multiplicative; the absolute-temperature offset is not inserted into a denominator. 1769.title: Thermal Model Uncertainty from Input Properties
1769.heading: Thermal Model Uncertainty from Input Properties
1769.content:
Thermal predictions inherit uncertainty from conductivity, heat capacity, density, emissivity, convection coefficients, source rates, and boundary temperatures. A precise numerical solution does not remove uncertainty in those physical inputs.

Ranges based on measurement accuracy or plausible operating variation can be explored with sweeps. Comparing their effect on the target output identifies which properties merit better characterization and prevents insignificant numerical detail from obscuring dominant [[Thermophysical Material Characterization|material uncertainty]].

1772.title: Thermal Model Benchmarking
1772.heading: Thermal Model Benchmarking
1772.content:
A thermal benchmark is a case with an analytical solution, trusted numerical result, or controlled experiment against which a model can be compared. Simple geometry and conditions isolate errors that are difficult to diagnose in a complete multiphysics system.

The comparison should use the same properties, dimensions, initial state, and boundary assumptions. Agreement with a [[Lumped-Capacity Cooling of Hot Water|lumped model]], for example, supports only the regime where its uniform-temperature assumption is valid and does not validate unrelated flow or radiation features.

1775.title: Thermal Mesh Refinement
1775.heading: Thermal Mesh Refinement
1775.content:
Thermal meshes need smaller elements where temperature changes rapidly, geometry has sharp features, materials meet, or boundary flux is concentrated. Regions with smooth, slowly varying fields can use larger elements without the same loss of accuracy.

Refinement should be driven by the output of interest rather than image smoothness. Repeated solutions with decreasing element size form a [[Mesh Independence Study|mesh-independence study]] that identifies when additional spatial resolution no longer changes the engineering conclusion appreciably.

1778.title: Thermal Management Goals
1778.heading: Thermal Management Goals
1778.content:
Thermal management uses analysis to keep temperatures, gradients, and heat-transfer rates within acceptable limits. The objective may be to remove waste heat, preserve warmth, control a process cycle, prevent damage, or make a design more energy efficient.

The required output should be stated before model construction: a maximum temperature, heating time, spatial uniformity, heat loss, or another measurable quantity. That objective guides [[Dominant Physics Selection for Thermal Problems|physics selection]], resolution, validation evidence, and the level of detail worth adding.

1781.sourceSearchName: thermal initial condition thermal initial condition
1781.title: Thermal Initial Condition
1781.heading: Thermal Initial Condition
1781.content:
An initial condition defines the temperature field from which a time-dependent thermal solution begins. It may be uniform, vary by domain, or come from a preceding study that has established a physically meaningful state.

Initial temperature affects the early transient and can influence nonlinear solver convergence. It is not a substitute for a [[Thermal Boundary Condition|boundary condition]], which governs interaction over time; the initial condition specifies the state at the starting instant only.

1784.heading: Thermal Imaging Validation of Hot Tea
1784.content:
The hot-tea case compares modeled surface temperatures with thermal-camera observations of a cup cooling over time. Matching the geometry, initial state, ambient conditions, and observation locations turns a familiar system into a controlled validation exercise.

Differences between prediction and observation expose uncertain convection coefficients, material assumptions, and measurement limits. The exercise demonstrates that increasing geometric or multiphysics detail is useful only when [[Comparing Thermal Simulation with Infrared Measurements|independent evidence]] tests the result.

1787.sourceSearchName: thermal imaging calibration thermal imaging calibration
1787.title: Thermal Imaging Calibration
1787.heading: Thermal Imaging Calibration
1787.content:
An infrared camera converts received radiative signals into apparent temperature using internal assumptions about emissivity and instrument response. Calibration against a black-body source of known temperature and emissivity checks that conversion over the measurement range.

User calibration can support an experiment, but it does not replace manufacturer adjustment of the camera's internal parameters. Credible [[Comparing Thermal Simulation with Infrared Measurements|simulation comparison]] must also account for resolution, accuracy, surface emissivity, viewing geometry, and ambient reflections.

1790.sourceSearchName: thermal expansion characterization thermal expansion characterization
1790.title: Thermal Expansion Characterization
1790.heading: Thermal Expansion Characterization
1790.content:
Thermomechanical analysis applies a small load while recording a specimen's dimensional change through a temperature cycle. The response yields strain and can be used to infer temperature-dependent elastic or viscoelastic behavior.

A dilatometer measures expansion more directly, and the thermal expansion coefficient relates relative dimensional or volumetric change to temperature. These properties become important when a thermal field is passed into a structural model or when expansion affects contact and [[Thermal Boundary Condition|boundary behavior]].

When an expansion coefficient is reported per degree on another temperature scale, its reciprocal-temperature unit must be converted with the interval size, not with the offset used for an absolute temperature reading. Pryor's unit-conversion example treats Fahrenheit and Celsius differences separately from thermometer values. See [[Temperature Readings versus Intervals]].
